newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.Africa credit growth seen slower in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.Africa credit growth seen slower in Nov.

text.p: South African consumers' appetite for credit is expected to have diminished in November marking the start of a downtrend expected to continue well into 1997, economists said on Friday.

The Reserve Bank will release private sector credit extension data next Thursday at 1500 GMT and a Reuters poll of economists forecast a year-on-year increase of 18.2 percent compared with 18.86 percent growth in October.
Economists said the main reason they were expecting a slowdown in growth in credit demand was technical.
"We are coming off a relatively high base from the corresponding month a year ago," Huysamer Stals economist Johan Rossouw said.

High interest rates are expected to have begun making inroads into the country's credit binge, although the last rate hike on November 21 was likely to have had only a slight impact on the month's data, economists said.
ABN Amro economist Anastasia Gekis said she believed October's shock 18.96 percent rise in credit extension was a peak which would be trimmed in November as a result of high interest rates.

Absa Treasury economist Charles Jonker agreed: "Our view on instalment sales and leases, mortgage advances and overdrafts and loans, is that we see a modest but downward trend from now onwards as the overall consumption economy is definitely fairly subdued due to the interest rate hikes.
"December could see a slight uptick because of seasonal factors, but the underlying economic trend is for overall consumption to move lower," Jonker added.
The credit data will be accompanied by money supply statistics which are expected to show a slowdown to 15.5 percent growth in November from a preliminary 15.96 percent in October.
Rossouw noted that as in the case of credit extension, latest money supply data would be calculated off a high base after rising 2.3 percent month-on-month last year.
The data would be influenced to a large degree by the government deposits component of money supply.

Although a high base figure in November 1995 would accentuate a drop in the growth rate this November, "an even more dramatic fall in money supply growth in November will probably be hampered by an expected turnaround in the figure for government deposits resulting in an inflow of money into the system," Rossouw said.
Government deposits increased by 4.176 billion rand in October.

Tertia Jacobs, gilts analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak, said she expected government deposits in the exchequer and tax and loan accounts at the Reserve Bank and banks to have dropped substantially in the month as a result of interest payments, the redemption of government's R146 stock and private sector credit extension to inhibit any fall in the money supply.
